    E03 — Earthing grid of a high-voltage substation in two-layer soil¶

    This case study takes the mesh earthing grid of an outdoor high-voltage substation through the touch-voltage verification of EN 50522:2022, in two-layer soil. It is written for grounding engineers who know the standard and IEEE Std 80 and want to see how groundfield answers the design questions, which engine to trust for which quantity, and how far the numbers carry.

    Questions this example answers

    1. What is the earthing impedance \(Z_E\) of the grid, and how much does the two-layer soil change it against a homogeneous estimate?
    2. Which earth potential rise \(U_E\), and which touch and step voltages, does an earth-fault current of 2 kA cause?
    3. Does the design meet the permissible touch voltage for a fault cleared in 0.5 s, and what would make it pass?
    4. Is the discretisation fine enough, and how do image_2layer, mom and the closed-form estimates compare?
    5. How do the layer contrast and the depth of the interface change the results?

    The tutorials T02 (layered soil), T08 (touch and step voltages) and T09 (engines and convergence) introduce the functions used here. This example applies them to one installation.

    Runtime: about 70 s.

    1. The installation and the soil¶

    Part Model Note
    Grid 60 m × 40 m, 12 × 8 meshes of 5 m 22 conductors, 1060 m
    Burial depth 0.8 m
    Conductor round copper, radius 6 mm 113 mm²
    Rods 4 × 3 m at the corners, radius 8 mm from 0.8 m to 3.8 m depth
    Earth-fault current \(I_E\) = 2 kA at 50 Hz flows from the grid into the soil
    Fault duration \(t_f\) = 0.5 s clearing time of the protection

    The earth-fault current \(I_E\) is the part of the fault current that leaves the grid through the soil. The rest returns to the source over the earth wires of the overhead lines and the screens of the cables. In a real study \(I_E\) follows from the network's fault currents and these reduction factors; here it is an assumption.

    The soil. A two-layer soil has an upper layer of resistivity \(\rho_1\) and thickness \(h_1\) over a half-space of resistivity \(\rho_2\). The interface reflects part of the current field with the factor

    \[ K = \frac{\rho_2 - \rho_1}{\rho_2 + \rho_1}, \qquad -1 < K < 1 . \]

    We take two soils with the same two resistivities in reverse order:

    Soil \(\rho_1\) \(h_1\) \(\rho_2\) \(K\) For example
    A 300 Ω·m 2.5 m 50 Ω·m −0.71 dry sand over groundwater
    B 50 Ω·m 2.5 m 300 Ω·m +0.71 loam over dry gravel or rock

    The grid lies in the upper layer in both soils; the rods reach 1.3 m into the lower one.

    Modelling choices¶

    • The grid is one grid_mesh electrode: its 22 conductors are straight wires, connected at every crossing.
    • The rods are separate rod electrodes, bonded to the grid by ideal conductors (create_conductor without a cross-section). An ideal bond merges the electrodes into one cluster at one potential; the route of the bond does not matter.
    • One potential for the whole grid. groundfield treats an electrode as an equipotential body: the resistance and inductance of the copper are neglected. That is the usual assumption of grid design (IEEE Std 80 makes it too) for a compact copper grid at 50 Hz.
    • The source is a current \(I_E\) into the grid that returns at remote earth. The problem is linear, so every voltage scales with \(I_E\).
    • The touched parts. All metal structures in the yard (steel supports, equipment frames) are bonded to the grid, and people may stand anywhere inside the yard. The yard fence runs on the line of the outer conductor and is bonded to the grid; people outside the fence stand 1 m from it.

    The engines¶

    Two engines solve thin wires in two-layer soil with the Tagg/Sunde image series:

    • image_2layer (what the default image runs for two-layer soil) gives every straight wire one uniform leakage current and integrates its potential exactly (line kernel). Its impedances are within about 1–2 % of mom, but near grids its surface potential is only impedance-grade: it cannot let the current crowd towards the ends of each wire, and it warns with UniformCurrentFieldWarning.
    • mom gives every segment its own current (piecewise constant, point matching at the segment midpoints, point kernel), so the current concentrates at the edges and corners of the grid as it does in reality. Its touch and step voltages are field-grade.

    We therefore compute everything with mom and use image_2layer and mom_sommerfeld (the same discretisation, with the layered Green's function as a Sommerfeld integral) as cross-checks in section 8. fem is not used: its three-dimensional model needed 75–140 s and 4.3 GB for a station with 28 m of wire (fem engine page), and this grid has 1072 m.

    2. Build the model¶

    One function builds the earthing system, so that the design variants of section 7 differ only in their arguments. The segment length DS of 1 m is justified in section 3.

    In [1]:

    import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import groundfield as gf
from groundfield.references import dwight1936, ieee80

print("groundfield", gf.__version__)
T_START = time.perf_counter()

I_E = 2000.0  # A, earth-fault current from the grid into the soil
T_F = 0.5  # s, fault duration
SIZE = (60.0, 40.0)  # m
MESHES = (12, 8)  # 5 m x 5 m meshes
DEPTH = 0.8  # m, burial depth of the grid
ROD_LENGTH = 3.0  # m
DS = 1.0  # m, segment length of mom (section 3)

SOILS = {
    "A": gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=300.0, rho_2=50.0, h_1=2.5),  # resistive over conductive
    "B": gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=50.0, rho_2=300.0, h_1=2.5),  # conductive over resistive
}
for name, soil in SOILS.items():
    K = (soil.rho_2 - soil.rho_1) / (soil.rho_2 + soil.rho_1)
    print(
        f"soil {name}: {soil.rho_1:.0f} over {soil.rho_2:.0f} Ohm m, h_1 = {soil.h_1} m, K = {K:+.3f}"
    )

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    def substation(
    soil, *, meshes=MESHES, rods="corners", rod_length=ROD_LENGTH, grading=False
):
    """The substation earth, fed with I_E: grid, bonded rods, optional grading conductor."""
    world = gf.create_world(soil=soil)
    lx, ly = SIZE
    gf.create_electrode(
        world,
        "grid_mesh",
        name="grid",
        corner=(0.0, 0.0, DEPTH),
        size=SIZE,
        n_x=meshes[0],
        n_y=meshes[1],
        wire_radius=0.006,
    )
    if rods == "corners":
        heads = [(0.0, 0.0), (lx, 0.0), (lx, ly), (0.0, ly)]
    else:  # "perimeter": every 10 m along the outer conductor
        heads = [(x, y) for x in np.arange(0.0, lx + 1.0, 10.0) for y in (0.0, ly)]
        heads += [(x, y) for y in np.arange(10.0, ly, 10.0) for x in (0.0, lx)]
    for k, (x, y) in enumerate(heads):
        gf.create_electrode(
            world,
            "rod",
            name=f"rod_{k}",
            position=(x, y, DEPTH),
            length=rod_length,
            wire_radius=0.008,
        )
        gf.create_conductor(
            world, name=f"bond_{k}", start="grid", end=f"rod_{k}"
        )  # ideal
    if grading:  # a closed conductor 1 m outside the grid, 0.5 m deep, bonded
        ring = [
            (-1.0, -1.0, 0.5),
            (lx + 1, -1.0, 0.5),
            (lx + 1, ly + 1, 0.5),
            (-1.0, ly + 1, 0.5),
        ]
        gf.create_electrode(
            world, "polyline", name="grading", vertices=ring, wire_radius=0.005
        )
        gf.create_conductor(world, name="bond_grading", start="grid", end="grading")
    gf.create_source(world, attached_to="grid", magnitude=I_E)
    return world


worlds = {name: substation(soil) for name, soil in SOILS.items()}

fig, (ax_plan, ax_side) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(10.0, 3.6), width_ratios=[1.0, 1.25]
)
gf.plot_world(worlds["A"], ax=ax_plan, show_conductors=False, title="plan view")
gf.plot_world(
    worlds["A"], plane="xz", ax=ax_side, show_conductors=False, title="side view"
)
ax_side.axhline(SOILS["A"].h_1, color="C1", ls="--", lw=1.0, label="layer interface")
ax_side.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()

    3. Is the discretisation fine enough?¶

    Before reading any number we check that it does not depend on the segment length. gf.convergence_study solves the same world with a ladder of segment lengths; a response function adds the touch voltages to the impedance. The helper touch returns the three touch voltages this example assesses:

    • outside: the largest value with the feet 1 m outside the grid, where people outside the fence stand (touch_voltage_envelope);
    • mesh: the largest value at the centres of the meshes, the mesh voltage of IEEE Std 80 (interior="meshes");
    • yard: the largest value anywhere inside the fence. It lies either at a mesh centre or on the fence line above the outer conductor, so touch also samples that line every metre. Section 5 confirms this against a dense map.

    touch_voltage_envelope places the feet on 24 rays from the centre of the grid and, by default, on the arc around each of its corners, where the touch voltage is largest. The rays alone miss the corners of a 60 m × 40 m rectangle (section 5 shows by how much). The mesh centres come from a second call with corners=False, whose interior points follow right after the 24 rays.

    mom needs segments shorter than about 2 m here. Its point form of the layered Green's function averages over ±0.387 segment lengths in depth; for longer segments that range would reach above the soil surface, and the engine refuses the world with BackendCapabilityError. The ladder therefore starts at 2 m.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    N_ANGLES = 24  # the envelope's default rays; the corner feet come on top
ALONG_X = np.arange(0.0, SIZE[0] + 1e-9, 1.0)
ALONG_Y = np.arange(0.0, SIZE[1] + 1e-9, 1.0)
FENCE_LINE = np.array(  # on the surface above the outer conductor, 1 m apart
    [(x, y, 0.0) for x in ALONG_X for y in (0.0, SIZE[1])]
    + [(x, y, 0.0) for y in ALONG_Y for x in (0.0, SIZE[0])]
)


def touch(result, world):
    """Largest |U_T| in V: outside the fence, at the mesh centres, anywhere in the yard."""
    _, u_out = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(result, world, electrode="grid")
    _, u_in = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(
        result, world, electrode="grid", interior="meshes", corners=False
    )
    u_line = np.abs(
        result.electrode_potentials["grid"][0] - result.potential(FENCE_LINE)
    )
    mesh = np.abs(u_in[N_ANGLES:]).max()
    return {
        "outside": np.abs(u_out).max(),
        "mesh": mesh,
        "yard": max(mesh, u_line.max()),
    }


def response(result, world, k):
    return {"Z_E": result.input_impedance()[k].real, **touch(result, world)}


mom = gf.create_engine(backend="mom", segment_length=DS)
ladder = [2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.25]
convergence = {
    name: gf.convergence_study(world, mom, segment_lengths=ladder, response=response)
    for name, world in worlds.items()
}
for name, df in convergence.items():
    finest = df.iloc[-1]
    print(f"soil {name}: deviation from the finest step (0.25 m)")
    print("  ds in m  segments  Z_E in Ohm    Z_E     U_T outside  U_T yard")
    for _, row in df.iterrows():
        dev = {q: row[q] / finest[q] - 1.0 for q in ("Z_E", "outside", "yard")}
        print(
            f"   {row['segment_length_m']:5.2f}   {row['n_segments']:6.0f}   {row['Z_E']:8.5f}"
            f"   {dev['Z_E']:+7.2%}    {dev['outside']:+7.2%}    {dev['yard']:+7.2%}"
        )
    N_ANGLES = 24 # the envelope's default rays; the corner feet come on top ALONG_X = np.arange(0.0, SIZE[0] + 1e-9, 1.0) ALONG_Y = np.arange(0.0, SIZE[1] + 1e-9, 1.0) FENCE_LINE = np.array( # on the surface above the outer conductor, 1 m apart [(x, y, 0.0) for x in ALONG_X for y in (0.0, SIZE[1])] + [(x, y, 0.0) for y in ALONG_Y for x in (0.0, SIZE[0])] ) def touch(result, world): """Largest |U_T| in V: outside the fence, at the mesh centres, anywhere in the yard.""" _, u_out = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(result, world, electrode="grid") _, u_in = gf.touch_voltage_envelope( result, world, electrode="grid", interior="meshes", corners=False ) u_line = np.abs( result.electrode_potentials["grid"][0] - result.potential(FENCE_LINE) ) mesh = np.abs(u_in[N_ANGLES:]).max() return { "outside": np.abs(u_out).max(), "mesh": mesh, "yard": max(mesh, u_line.max()), } def response(result, world, k): return {"Z_E": result.input_impedance()[k].real, **touch(result, world)} mom = gf.create_engine(backend="mom", segment_length=DS) ladder = [2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.25] convergence = { name: gf.convergence_study(world, mom, segment_lengths=ladder, response=response) for name, world in worlds.items() } for name, df in convergence.items(): finest = df.iloc[-1] print(f"soil {name}: deviation from the finest step (0.25 m)") print(" ds in m segments Z_E in Ohm Z_E U_T outside U_T yard") for _, row in df.iterrows(): dev = {q: row[q] / finest[q] - 1.0 for q in ("Z_E", "outside", "yard")} print( f" {row['segment_length_m']:5.2f} {row['n_segments']:6.0f} {row['Z_E']:8.5f}" f" {dev['Z_E']:+7.2%} {dev['outside']:+7.2%} {dev['yard']:+7.2%}" )

    Copied! 
    for df in convergence.values():
    at_ds = df[df["segment_length_m"] == DS].iloc[0]
    finest = df.iloc[-1]
    for q in ("Z_E", "outside", "yard"):
        assert abs(at_ds[q] / finest[q] - 1.0) < 0.01  # 1 m is within 1 % of 0.25 m
    assert np.all(np.diff(df["Z_E"]) > 0)  # the impedance rises monotonically
    for df in convergence.values(): at_ds = df[df["segment_length_m"] == DS].iloc[0] finest = df.iloc[-1] for q in ("Z_E", "outside", "yard"): assert abs(at_ds[q] / finest[q] - 1.0) < 0.01 # 1 m is within 1 % of 0.25 m assert np.all(np.diff(df["Z_E"]) > 0) # the impedance rises monotonically

    With 1 m segments the impedance is within 0.2 % of the 0.25 m value and the touch voltages within 0.6 %. The impedance rises steadily as the segments shrink: the point kernel of mom converges to a value slightly below the exact one (T09 shows it for a rod). The effect on the design is far smaller than the uncertainty of any soil model. We keep 1 m.

    4. Grid impedance and earth potential rise¶

    In homogeneous soil the impedance is proportional to the resistivity, \(Z_E = \rho\, z_1\). One solve gives the impedance per Ω·m, \(z_1\), and with it both homogeneous limits: \(\rho_1 z_1\) for a very thick and \(\rho_2 z_1\) for a very thin upper layer. The two-layer impedance must lie between them. The apparent resistivity \(\rho_a = Z_E / z_1\) is the homogeneous resistivity that would give the same impedance.

    Sverak's formula of IEEE Std 80 (2000, Eq. 57) is the engineering estimate for grids in homogeneous soil, with the total conductor length \(L_T\) (grid and rods), the area \(A\) and the depth \(h\):

    \[ R_g = \rho\left[\frac{1}{L_T} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{20A}}\left(1 + \frac{1}{1 + h\sqrt{20/A}}\right)\right]. \]

    With \(Z_E\) the earth potential rise is \(U_E = Z_E I_E\).

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    results = {name: mom.solve(world) for name, world in worlds.items()}
z_e = {name: res.input_impedance()[0].real for name, res in results.items()}
u_e = {name: abs(res.electrode_potentials["grid"][0]) for name, res in results.items()}

hom_world = substation(gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0))
homogeneous = mom.solve(hom_world)
z_1 = homogeneous.input_impedance()[0].real / 100.0  # Ohm per Ohm m
L_T = 13 * 40.0 + 9 * 60.0 + 4 * ROD_LENGTH  # m, grid conductors and rods
sverak_1 = ieee80.grid_resistance_sverak(
    1.0, total_conductor_length=L_T, area=2400.0, depth=DEPTH
)

print(
    f"homogeneous soil: z_1 = {z_1 * 1e3:.4f} mOhm per Ohm m (mom), "
    f"Sverak {sverak_1 * 1e3:.4f} ({sverak_1 / z_1 - 1:+.1%})"
)
print()
print("soil  Z_E (mom)    U_E at 2 kA  rho_2 limit  rho_1 limit  rho_a")
for name, soil in SOILS.items():
    print(
        f"  {name}   {z_e[name]:.4f} Ohm   {u_e[name]:6.0f} V    {soil.rho_2 * z_1:.4f} Ohm"

    Plausibility. Sverak's formula lies +8.9 % above mom in homogeneous soil, its usual accuracy for grids (T08 finds +11.8 % for a 20 m grid). It has no two-layer form, but the two-layer results lie between the homogeneous limits, as they must.

    What the soil does. The two soils contain the same resistivities, yet their impedances differ by a factor of 2.2. A 60 m × 40 m grid drives its current tens of metres deep, so it sees mainly the lower layer: the apparent resistivity is 88 Ω·m in soil A, near the 50 Ω·m of the bottom, and 195 Ω·m in soil B, nearer the 300 Ω·m of the bottom than the 50 Ω·m around the grid. A sounding that stops a few metres deep would misjudge this grid badly.

    The rods. The four corner rods carry only a few per cent of the current:

    A single 3 m rod alone would have 17 to 100 Ω, depending on the layer it stands in (Dwight's closed form for homogeneous soil): ten to a hundred times the impedance of the grid. And the corner rods stand in the potential well of the grid. Rods of 3 m therefore change \(Z_E\) little; section 7 shows what longer rods do.

    EN 50522 first. EN 50522:2022, 5.4.2, accepts the design without a touch-voltage calculation if \(U_E \le 2\,U_{Tp}\) (criterion C2), or if \(U_E \le 4\,U_{Tp}\) and the measures M of Annex E, Table E.1, are taken (C3). Otherwise (C4) the touch voltages must be shown to stay below the permissible value, by calculation or measurement. groundfield provides the permissible touch voltage \(U_{Tp}(t_f)\) of Table B.4 (gf.permissible_touch_voltage_en50522):

    Both soils lead to criterion C4: we compute the touch voltages.

    5. Touch voltages on the surface¶

    The touch voltage is the difference between the potential of the touched part, here the earth potential rise \(U_E\) of the grid, and the potential of the soil surface under the feet, 1 m away:

    \[ U_T = U_E - \varphi(\mathbf r_\text{feet}). \]

    This is the prospective (open-circuit) value: no body current flows. We evaluate the surface potential \(\varphi\) on a grid of points 0.5 m apart that covers the yard and 5 m around it, 141 × 101 points. The grid, the rods and the feeding point are symmetric about both centre lines, so one quarter (3621 points) is computed and mirrored. Inside the yard every point is a possible standing position next to a bonded structure, so the map is the touch voltage there. Outside, \(U_E - \varphi\) is a touch voltage only where a bonded part stands within 1 m: along the fence.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    x_q = np.arange(-5.0, SIZE[0] / 2 + 1e-9, 0.5)  # the lower left quarter
y_q = np.arange(-5.0, SIZE[1] / 2 + 1e-9, 0.5)
X_q, Y_q = np.meshgrid(x_q, y_q)
quarter = np.column_stack([X_q.ravel(), Y_q.ravel(), np.zeros(X_q.size)])
x = np.concatenate([x_q, SIZE[0] - x_q[-2::-1]])  # -5 ... 65 m
y = np.concatenate([y_q, SIZE[1] - y_q[-2::-1]])  # -5 ... 45 m
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
in_yard = (X >= 0.0) & (X <= SIZE[0]) & (Y >= 0.0) & (Y <= SIZE[1])


def mirror(q):
    """The full map from its lower left quarter."""
    half = np.hstack([q, q[:, -2::-1]])
    return np.vstack([half, half[-2::-1, :]])


u_map = {}
for name, res in results.items():
    phi = res.potential(quarter).reshape(X_q.shape)
    u_map[name] = mirror(np.abs(res.electrode_potentials["grid"][0] - phi))

limits = {name: touch(res, worlds[name]) for name, res in results.items()}
for name, u in u_map.items():
    k = np.argmax(np.where(in_yard, u, -np.inf))
    print(
        f"soil {name}: in the yard {u[in_yard].min():.0f} ... {u.flat[k]:.0f} V, the largest at "
        f"({X.flat[k]:.1f}, {Y.flat[k]:.1f}) m; above U_Tp on {np.sum(u[in_yard] > u_tp)} "
        f"of {in_yard.sum()} points; 1 m outside the grid up to {limits[name]['outside']:.0f} V"
    )
    x_q = np.arange(-5.0, SIZE[0] / 2 + 1e-9, 0.5) # the lower left quarter y_q = np.arange(-5.0, SIZE[1] / 2 + 1e-9, 0.5) X_q, Y_q = np.meshgrid(x_q, y_q) quarter = np.column_stack([X_q.ravel(), Y_q.ravel(), np.zeros(X_q.size)]) x = np.concatenate([x_q, SIZE[0] - x_q[-2::-1]]) # -5 ... 65 m y = np.concatenate([y_q, SIZE[1] - y_q[-2::-1]]) # -5 ... 45 m X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y) in_yard = (X >= 0.0) & (X <= SIZE[0]) & (Y >= 0.0) & (Y <= SIZE[1]) def mirror(q): """The full map from its lower left quarter.""" half = np.hstack([q, q[:, -2::-1]]) return np.vstack([half, half[-2::-1, :]]) u_map = {} for name, res in results.items(): phi = res.potential(quarter).reshape(X_q.shape) u_map[name] = mirror(np.abs(res.electrode_potentials["grid"][0] - phi)) limits = {name: touch(res, worlds[name]) for name, res in results.items()} for name, u in u_map.items(): k = np.argmax(np.where(in_yard, u, -np.inf)) print( f"soil {name}: in the yard {u[in_yard].min():.0f} ... {u.flat[k]:.0f} V, the largest at " f"({X.flat[k]:.1f}, {Y.flat[k]:.1f}) m; above U_Tp on {np.sum(u[in_yard] > u_tp)} " f"of {in_yard.sum()} points; 1 m outside the grid up to {limits[name]['outside']:.0f} V" )

    The colour scale ends at the largest touch voltage outside the fence. Farther out, \(U_E - \varphi\) keeps growing towards \(U_E\), but no bonded part stands there. The maps show the two faces of a two-layer soil:

    • In soil A (resistive over conductive) the surface potential sags in every mesh. The touch voltage in the yard lies between 217 V and 552 V, highest in the corner meshes; it is above \(U_{Tp}\) = 225 V almost everywhere (9786 of 9801 points).
    • In soil B (conductive over resistive) the conductive top layer spreads the current sideways and flattens the surface potential. In the yard only the corners exceed \(U_{Tp}\), with 301 V right above the corner conductor, although \(U_E\) is more than twice as high as in soil A.

    In both soils the largest touch voltage stands outside the corners, where the potential falls fastest. That is where mom matters: the current per metre is largest at the ends of the outer conductors.

    Two checks of the values outside the fence. The fence post at a corner, touched from outside along the diagonal, is the standing position of the envelope's maximum; and the 24 rays alone, without the corner feet, miss it:

    With the 24 rays alone the envelope reads 12 % low in soil A and 28 % low in soil B, on the unsafe side. This example found that gap; since release 2026.11.0 the envelope therefore also stands on the arc around every corner (corners=True, the default), and it agrees with the corner post. The rays alone happen to hit the corners of a square grid only, whose diagonals lie at multiples of 15°.

    6. Step voltages¶

    A person walking near the grid bridges the step voltage between two points 1 m apart,

    \[ U_S = \varphi(\mathbf r) - \varphi(\mathbf r + 1\,\mathrm m\;\hat{\mathbf e}). \]

    It is largest where the surface potential falls fastest, at the corners. We evaluate it along two lines out of the grid, the diagonal through a corner and the normal through the middle of a long side, from inside the outer mesh to 12 m outside. The step points outwards; the plot shows its magnitude.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    s = np.arange(-3.5, 12.0 + 1e-9, 0.1)  # m from the outer conductor, positive outside
lines = {
    "diagonal through the corner": ((0.0, 0.0), np.array([-1.0, -1.0]) / np.sqrt(2.0)),
    "normal through the middle of the long side": ((30.0, 0.0), np.array([0.0, -1.0])),
}

            [origin[0] + s * e[0], origin[1] + s * e[1], np.zeros_like(s)]

    The largest step voltages, 214 V in soil A and 185 V in soil B, begin at the corner and stay below the touch voltages. EN 50522:2022 rarely asks for them, and Annex A.3 gives the reason: the permissible step voltages are much higher than the permissible touch voltages, because the current from foot to foot passes the heart with a heart-current factor of only 0.04. The standard asks for the step voltages at the boundary of an installation only for high earth potential rises, and names \(U_E > 20\,U_{Tp}\) as an example (5.4.2, note 1); here \(U_E\) is below \(16\,U_{Tp}\) in both soils. groundfield has no permissible step voltage; it is not needed here.

    7. Assessment against EN 50522, and what makes the design pass¶

    The permissible touch voltage across the body for \(t_f\) = 0.5 s is \(U_{Tp}\) = 225 V. EN 50522 allows additional resistances in the body circuit: the hand \(R_H\), the footwear \(R_{F1}\), and the soil or surface layer under the feet with \(R_{F2} = 1.5\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\rho_s\). The permissible prospective touch voltage (Annex B.4) is then

    \[ U_{vTp} = U_{Tp}(t_f) + \frac{I_B(t_f)}{HF}\,\bigl(R_H + R_{F1} + 1.5\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\rho_s\bigr), \]

    with the permissible body current \(I_B(t_f)\) of Table B.1 and the heart-current factor \(HF\) = 1 (hand to feet). We compare with three levels: bare contact (\(U_{Tp}\)); shoes of 1000 Ω on the natural topsoil; and a layer of crushed rock of 3000 Ω·m (an assumed wet value) without shoes.

    In [15]:
    Copied!

        T_F, R_F1=1000.0, rho_s=soil.rho_1
    )
    levels[name] = {"bare": u_tp, "shoes": u_vtp_shoes, "rock": u_vtp_rock}

    The base design fails the bare criterion in both soils: in soil A everywhere, in soil B at the corners of the yard and outside the fence. Shoes on the natural soil save only the yard of soil B. Crushed rock helps where it lies: inside the yard it covers the yard in both soils; for the people outside the fence it would have to continue as a strip outside.

    How short would the clearing time have to be? \(U_{Tp}(t_f)\) falls with the fault duration; the base design passes for faults cleared before the curve drops below its largest touch voltage:

    Only a very fast protection would save the base design (0.06 s in soil A, 0.22 s in soil B). So we change the earthing system, with two measures of common practice:

    1. a grading conductor: a closed conductor 1 m outside the grid and 0.5 m deep, bonded to it, so that people outside the fence stand above a conductor;
    2. in addition, perimeter rods: 20 rods of 6 m every 10 m along the outer conductor instead of the four corner rods; they reach 4.3 m into the lower layer.

    The feet above the grading conductor are only 0.5 m from it, closer than a 1 m segment is long, so the variants are solved with 0.5 m segments. The base design at 0.5 m is already in the convergence study of section 3.

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    VARIANTS = {
    "grading conductor": {"grading": True},
    "grading + perimeter rods": {
        "grading": True,
        "rods": "perimeter",
        "rod_length": 6.0,
    },
}
fine = gf.create_engine(backend="mom", segment_length=0.5)
variants = {}
for name, soil in SOILS.items():
    base = convergence[name].set_index("segment_length_m").loc[0.5]
    variants[name, "base design"] = {
        q: base[q] for q in ("Z_E", "outside", "mesh", "yard")
    }
    for label, options in VARIANTS.items():
        world = substation(soil, **options)
        res = fine.solve(world)
        variants[name, label] = {
            "Z_E": res.input_impedance()[0].real,
            **touch(res, world),
        }

        f"    {v['outside']:5.0f}   {verdict}"
    )

    What the variants show:

    • Soil B needs only the grading conductor. It raises the surface potential where the people outside the fence stand and pulls the value there from 486 V to 186 V, the yard from 300 V to 121 V: the design passes on bare contact. The perimeter rods add little in soil B, because their lower part stands in the 300 Ω·m bottom.
    • Soil A is harder: the resistive top layer leaves a large share of \(U_E\) between the grid and the surface everywhere. The grading conductor alone brings the fence to 309 V and leaves the yard at 455 V. The perimeter rods reach the conductive bottom and lower \(U_E\) itself, from 1466 V to 1138 V; the fence then passes on bare contact (189 V), but the corner meshes still have 262 V. With crushed rock in the yard (\(U_{vTp}\) = 1125 V), or shoes on the natural soil (\(U_{vTp}\) = 515 V), the design passes. Without either, smaller meshes near the corners would be the remaining measure: they lower the mesh voltage at the price of more conductor.

    EN 50522 verifies a design by the calculated or measured touch voltages of the installation as built. These numbers choose the measures; the verification still follows.

    8. Cross-checks: image_2layer, mom_sommerfeld and closed forms¶

    The same two worlds, solved with the default engine (image, which runs image_2layer for two-layer soil). Its touch voltages trigger the UniformCurrentFieldWarning; we record it and print it once.

    For the impedance the two engines agree within 1.6 %: either serves a study of \(Z_E\) and \(U_E\). For the touch voltages the uniform current per wire of image_2layer overestimates, by up to 45 % at the mesh centres of soil B. Its step voltage at the corner is 4.5 % high in soil A but 4.7 % low in soil B, on the unsafe side. With a conductive top layer the current crowds strongly towards the ends of every conductor, which one current per wire cannot follow. Assess touch and step voltages near a grid with mom.

    mom_sommerfeld evaluates the layered Green's function by numerical Sommerfeld quadrature instead of the image series, on the same discretisation as mom. Their agreement checks the series in this strong contrast:

)

    Closed forms. The library offers Sverak's formula of IEEE Std 80 for the grid resistance in homogeneous soil (section 4: +8.9 % above mom) and Dwight's formulas for single electrodes (section 4: the rods). It has no closed form for mesh or step voltages; IEEE Std 80's \(K_m\), \(K_i\) and \(K_s\) factors are not implemented. The homogeneous limits of the next section are the strongest independent check of the two-layer results.

    9. Layer contrast and interface depth¶

    First the interface depth: the two contrasts of soils A and B with \(h_1\) from 1.5 m to 50 m. The touch voltages are shown relative to \(U_E\), as the fraction of the earth potential rise that a person bridges.

    In [23]:
    Copied! 
    H_1 = [1.5, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 50.0]
PAIRS = {
    "300 over 50 Ω·m (K < 0)": (300.0, 50.0),
    "50 over 300 Ω·m (K > 0)": (50.0, 300.0),
}


def study(soil):
    """Z_E and the largest touch voltages outside and in the yard, as fractions of U_E."""
    world = substation(soil)
    res = mom.solve(world)
    z = res.input_impedance()[0].real
    t_v = touch(res, world)
    return z, t_v["outside"] / (z * I_E), t_v["yard"] / (z * I_E)


hom_touch = touch(homogeneous, hom_world)
hom_fraction = {q: v / (100.0 * z_1 * I_E) for q, v in hom_touch.items()}
depth_sweep = {
    label: np.array([study(gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=r1, rho_2=r2, h_1=h)) for h in H_1])
    for label, (r1, r2) in PAIRS.items()
}

fig, (ax_z, ax_u) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.0, 3.8))
for k, (label, values) in enumerate(depth_sweep.items()):
    r1, r2 = PAIRS[label]
    ax_z.semilogx(H_1, values[:, 0], "o-", color=f"C{k}", label=label)
    ax_z.axhline(r1 * z_1, color=f"C{k}", ls="--", lw=0.8)
    ax_z.axhline(r2 * z_1, color=f"C{k}", ls=":", lw=0.8)
    ax_u.semilogx(H_1, values[:, 1], "o-", color=f"C{k}", label=f"{label}, outside")
    ax_u.semilogx(H_1, values[:, 2], "s--", color=f"C{k}", label=f"{label}, yard")
for q, ls in (("outside", "-"), ("yard", "--")):
    ax_u.axhline(hom_fraction[q], color="grey", ls=ls, lw=0.8)
ax_z.set_ylabel(r"$Z_E$ in Ω (dashed: $\rho_1$, dotted: $\rho_2$)")
ax_u.set_ylabel(r"$U_T / U_E$ (grey: homogeneous soil)")
for ax in (ax_z, ax_u):
    ax.axvline(DEPTH + ROD_LENGTH, color="k", lw=0.6)
    ax.set_xticks(H_1, [f"{h:g}" for h in H_1])
    ax.minorticks_off()
    ax.set_xlabel("thickness of the upper layer $h_1$ in m (black: rod ends)")
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax_z.legend(fontsize=7)
ax_u.legend(fontsize=7)
fig.tight_layout()
print(
    f"homogeneous soil: U_T / U_E = {hom_fraction['outside']:.3f} (outside), "
    f"{hom_fraction['yard']:.3f} (yard)"
)
for label, values in depth_sweep.items():
    r1, r2 = PAIRS[label]
    print(
        f"{label}: Z_E at h_1 = 50 m {values[-1, 0]:.4f} Ohm (rho_1 limit {r1 * z_1:.4f} Ohm); "
        f"U_T / U_E outside {values[:, 1].min():.3f} ... {values[:, 1].max():.3f}"
    )
    H_1 = [1.5, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 50.0] PAIRS = { "300 over 50 Ω·m (K < 0)": (300.0, 50.0), "50 over 300 Ω·m (K > 0)": (50.0, 300.0), } def study(soil): """Z_E and the largest touch voltages outside and in the yard, as fractions of U_E.""" world = substation(soil) res = mom.solve(world) z = res.input_impedance()[0].real t_v = touch(res, world) return z, t_v["outside"] / (z * I_E), t_v["yard"] / (z * I_E) hom_touch = touch(homogeneous, hom_world) hom_fraction = {q: v / (100.0 * z_1 * I_E) for q, v in hom_touch.items()} depth_sweep = { label: np.array([study(gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=r1, rho_2=r2, h_1=h)) for h in H_1]) for label, (r1, r2) in PAIRS.items() } fig, (ax_z, ax_u) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.0, 3.8)) for k, (label, values) in enumerate(depth_sweep.items()): r1, r2 = PAIRS[label] ax_z.semilogx(H_1, values[:, 0], "o-", color=f"C{k}", label=label) ax_z.axhline(r1 * z_1, color=f"C{k}", ls="--", lw=0.8) ax_z.axhline(r2 * z_1, color=f"C{k}", ls=":", lw=0.8) ax_u.semilogx(H_1, values[:, 1], "o-", color=f"C{k}", label=f"{label}, outside") ax_u.semilogx(H_1, values[:, 2], "s--", color=f"C{k}", label=f"{label}, yard") for q, ls in (("outside", "-"), ("yard", "--")): ax_u.axhline(hom_fraction[q], color="grey", ls=ls, lw=0.8) ax_z.set_ylabel(r"$Z_E$ in Ω (dashed: $\rho_1$, dotted: $\rho_2$)") ax_u.set_ylabel(r"$U_T / U_E$ (grey: homogeneous soil)") for ax in (ax_z, ax_u): ax.axvline(DEPTH + ROD_LENGTH, color="k", lw=0.6) ax.set_xticks(H_1, [f"{h:g}" for h in H_1]) ax.minorticks_off() ax.set_xlabel("thickness of the upper layer $h_1$ in m (black: rod ends)") ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3) ax_z.legend(fontsize=7) ax_u.legend(fontsize=7) fig.tight_layout() print( f"homogeneous soil: U_T / U_E = {hom_fraction['outside']:.3f} (outside), " f"{hom_fraction['yard']:.3f} (yard)" ) for label, values in depth_sweep.items(): r1, r2 = PAIRS[label] print( f"{label}: Z_E at h_1 = 50 m {values[-1, 0]:.4f} Ohm (rho_1 limit {r1 * z_1:.4f} Ohm); " f"U_T / U_E outside {values[:, 1].min():.3f} ... {values[:, 1].max():.3f}" )

    The impedance moves monotonically from the \(\rho_2\) limit (thin upper layer) towards the \(\rho_1\) limit (thick upper layer), and slowly: even at \(h_1\) = 50 m it has not reached it, because the grid's current field reaches deeper than its size.

    The touch-voltage fraction behaves the other way round, and that is the design lesson. With a resistive top over a conductive bottom (\(K < 0\)) a person outside the fence bridges up to 0.45 of \(U_E\), 1.7 times the homogeneous value: the current leaves the grid downwards, and the surface above it is pulled towards the low potential of the conductive bottom. With a conductive top over a resistive bottom (\(K > 0\)) the fraction drops below the homogeneous value. A low \(Z_E\) in soil A therefore does not mean low touch voltages, and a high \(Z_E\) in soil B does not mean high ones.

    Now the contrast itself, with a 100 Ω·m upper layer of 2.5 m and the lower layer from 10 to 1000 Ω·m:

    Across the contrasts \(Z_E\) grows by a factor of 24, while the fraction \(U_T/U_E\) outside the fence falls from 0.51 to 0.12. The touch voltage itself, \(U_T = Z_E I_E \cdot (U_T/U_E)\), grows by a factor of 5.5 only. Scaling the homogeneous fraction with the two-layer impedance would understate the touch voltage by half over the conductive bottom (\(K\) = −0.82) and overstate it 2.3 times over the resistive one (\(K\) = +0.82): wrong in both directions, and on the unsafe side where the bottom conducts.

    10. What this means for the design¶

    • Measure deep. A 60 m × 40 m grid sees the soil to tens of metres: its apparent resistivity is 88 Ω·m in soil A and 195 Ω·m in soil B. The sounding must reach depths of the order of the grid size.
    • The earth potential rise is not the hazard. Soil B has more than twice the \(U_E\) of soil A but lower touch voltages (486 V against 710 V outside the fence, 301 V against 552 V in the yard). Calculate the touch voltages (EN 50522 criterion C4) with a field-grade engine.
    • Use mom for touch and step voltages near a grid. image_2layer is fine for \(Z_E\) (within 1.6 % here) but overestimates the mesh voltages by up to 45 % and, in soil B, underestimates the step voltage at a corner.
    • Check the corners. The largest touch voltages stand 1 m outside a corner and, in soil B, right above the corner conductor. The envelope samples the corners outside; touch points at the corner posts or a dense map cover the rest.
    • The measures depend on the soil. In soil B a grading conductor outside the fence is enough. In soil A rods into the conductive bottom, the grading conductor and a surface layer in the yard (or smaller corner meshes) are needed.

    Limits of this example¶

    • Equipotential grid, no inductive effects. The copper's resistance and inductance are neglected, and so is the inductive coupling to the faulted line. For grids of several hundred metres, steel conductors or frequencies well above 50 Hz the potential varies along the grid, and this model does not show it.
    • The earth-fault current is given. The split of the fault current between the grid, the earth wires and the cable screens (the reduction factors) is not computed; tutorial T06 shows how a connected network shares the current. Transferred potentials (cable screens, pipes, a fence that leaves the site) are not assessed.
    • The soil is two horizontal layers from an assumed sounding, without seasonal variation or frozen ground. Three or more layers need mom_sommerfeld, and FieldResult.potential raises NotImplementedError for them, so touch voltages in three-layer soil are out of reach.
    • Crushed rock enters only as a resistance under the feet (\(R_{F2}\) of EN 50522). Its thin high-resistivity layer would be a third soil layer, which the field model does not include.
    • Point kernel of mom. Its impedance changes by about 0.2 % from 1 m to 0.25 m segments here and stays slightly below the exact value; the surface potential directly above a shallow conductor needs segments shorter than the conductor's depth (section 7).
    • EN 50522 in the library: the permissible touch voltage of Table B.4 (80 V beyond 10 s) and the prospective value of Annex B.4. The permissible step voltage (Annex A.3), the measures M (Annex E) and the global earthing system (criterion C1) are not implemented; IEEE Std 80 enters only through Sverak's resistance formula.
    • No fem reference. The 3-D model of fem is the independent reference for small clusters; a grid with 1 km of wire is far beyond its default node limit. The cross-checks here are image_2layer, mom_sommerfeld, the homogeneous limits and the closed forms.

    See also the how-to assess touch voltages and the known limitations.
